questions.prompt: Three extra nucleotides are inserted together, right between two codons in the middle of a gene. Based on how reading frames work, what is the most likely result?

options.text: Every amino acid after the insertion is wrong, just as with a single insertion
Nothing changes, since insertions are removed before translation
The protein is cut off at the insertion, since three nucleotides always form a stop codon
One extra amino acid is added, and the codons after it are read normally, since the frame is restored

questions.explanation: Codons are read in threes. Adding exactly three nucleotides between codons adds one codon but doesn't shift the frame.

questions.prompt: A gene has a single-nucleotide deletion at codon 10 and a single-nucleotide insertion at codon 14. What happens to the protein?

options.text: Only codon 10 and codon 14 are changed; the codons between them are read correctly
Nothing is changed, since a deletion and an insertion always cancel exactly at the same codon
Codons 10 through 14 are misread, but the frame is restored after the insertion, so later amino acids are correct
Every codon from 10 to the end is misread, since two frameshifts double the damage

questions.explanation: The deletion shifts the frame; the insertion shifts it back. Only the stretch between them is read in the wrong frame.

questions.prompt: In a repressible operon, a mutation stops the corepressor from binding the repressor protein. What happens to the genes?

options.text: They switch on and off normally, since the corepressor isn't needed
They stay ON all the time, even when the product is plentiful, since the repressor can never be activated
They turn on only when the corepressor is present
They stay OFF all the time, since the repressor binds the operator permanently

questions.explanation: In a repressible operon the repressor is made inactive; the corepressor is what activates it to shut the genes off.

questions.prompt: A mutation in the lac operon's PROMOTER stops RNA polymerase from binding there. What happens when lactose is added?

options.text: The lac genes still aren't expressed — lactose inactivates the repressor, but RNA polymerase still can't bind, so the cell can't use the lactose
The lac genes are expressed all the time, even with no lactose, since the repressor can no longer block a damaged promoter
The repressor gene stops being expressed instead, so the lac genes switch on and lactose is broken down as usual
The lac genes are expressed normally, since lactose binds the damaged promoter and pulls RNA polymerase onto it

questions.explanation: Removing the repressor doesn't help if RNA polymerase can't bind the promoter. No transcription → no lactase enzymes.

questions.prompt: A hospital room is exposed to UV light for 30 minutes instead of 5. Why is the longer exposure much more likely to kill the microbes?

options.text: The longer the exposure, the more thymine dimers build up, so it becomes more likely that one damages an essential gene
Longer exposure turns the thymine dimers into silent mutations, which shut down every gene in the cell
UV only begins forming thymine dimers after about 30 minutes, so the 5-minute exposure does no DNA damage at all
Longer exposure heats the room's surfaces enough to denature the microbes' proteins, the way an autoclave does

questions.explanation: UV keeps creating thymine dimers wherever two Ts sit next to each other; statistically, an error eventually hits an important gene.

questions.prompt: Which DNA stretch is most vulnerable to forming a UV thymine dimer?

options.text: 5'–ATATATA–3'
5'–GCGCGCG–3'
5'–CAGTCAG–3'
5'–GATTTAC–3'

questions.explanation: A thymine dimer forms where two thymines sit next to each other on the same strand. Only GATTTAC has adjacent Ts.

questions.prompt: Why can a bacterium begin translating an mRNA before transcription of that mRNA is even finished?

options.text: Bacteria have no nucleus, so transcription and translation can happen at the same time in the same place
Bacterial ribosomes are located inside the nucleus, right next to the DNA
Bacterial mRNA is double-stranded, so one strand can be translated while the other is copied
Bacteria skip transcription and translate their DNA directly

questions.explanation: Instructor slides: in prokaryotes, transcription and translation can occur simultaneously; in eukaryotes they are separated in space and time.

questions.prompt: A ribosome mistakenly starts reading one nucleotide AFTER the AUG start codon. What would the result look like?

options.text: No protein at all, since translation can only begin at the 5' end
Like a silent mutation — the protein would be the same minus one amino acid
Like a frameshift — nearly every codon would be read wrong, because the reading frame is off
Like a nonsense mutation — the protein would stop at the next codon

questions.explanation: The start codon sets the reading frame. Starting one nucleotide off shifts every codon that follows.

questions.prompt: Of the 64 codons, 3 are stop codons. How many codons specify an amino acid?
questions.explanation: 64 − 3 stop codons = 61 codons for the 20 amino acids (AUG = Met is also the start codon).

questions.prompt: Why is the lac operon described as a self-regulating, negative-feedback system?

options.text: The enzymes it makes destroy the repressor protein, so the genes stay on until the cell divides
The enzymes it makes break down lactose — the very inducer that turned the genes on — so the genes shut themselves back off
The cell destroys its lactase mRNA, which deletes the lac genes from the chromosome
Lactose builds up until it physically blocks the promoter, shutting the genes off

questions.explanation: Lactose (inducer) turns the genes on → lactase digests lactose → no inducer left → the repressor becomes active again → genes off.

questions.prompt: Which statement comparing transcription and DNA replication is FALSE?

options.text: Transcription makes a single-stranded RNA copy; replication makes double-stranded DNA.
Transcription is carried out by DNA polymerase, the same enzyme that builds DNA in replication.
RNA polymerase falls off at the terminator sequence.
RNA polymerase reads only one DNA strand, the template strand.
After RNA polymerase passes, the DNA zips back together.

questions.explanation: False — transcription is done by RNA polymerase, which unzips the DNA and builds RNA.

questions.prompt: Which statement about substitution mutation types (instructor slides) is FALSE?

options.text: A nonsense mutation changes one amino acid into a different amino acid.
All three are point mutations, because they involve a single nucleotide.
A missense mutation changes one amino acid into another.
A nonsense mutation changes an amino acid codon into a premature stop codon.
A silent mutation causes no change to the amino acid.

questions.explanation: False — that describes missense. Nonsense creates a premature stop codon.

questions.prompt: Which statement about tRNA is FALSE?

options.text: A tRNA is a single-stranded RNA that folds into a clover-leaf shape.
The amino acid a tRNA carries depends on its anticodon.
Each tRNA can be used only once and is destroyed after delivering its amino acid.
tRNAs bring amino acids to the ribosome during translation.
A tRNA's anticodon binds an mRNA codon by complementary base pairing.

questions.explanation: False — tRNAs are recyclable; after delivering an amino acid, a tRNA leaves to pick up another.

questions.prompt: E. coli growing with no lactose is moved into a medium where lactose is the only sugar. Describe what happens at the lac operon from the moment lactose appears until it has all been used up.
questions.explanation: Before lactose: the regulatory gene constantly makes active repressor, which sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase from the promoter, so the lac genes are off (inducible = default off). When lactose arrives, it acts as the inducer: it binds the repressor, changes its shape, and inactivates it, so the repressor leaves the operator. RNA polymerase binds the promoter and transcribes the three lac genes; the mRNA is translated into lactase enzymes that break down lactose. As lactose runs out, nothing is left to bind the repressor; it returns to its active shape, binds the operator again, and transcription stops — the genes turn themselves off.

questions.prompt: Trace one bacterial gene from DNA to a folded protein. Name the molecules and enzymes involved in each step, and explain why the mRNA is destroyed at the end.
questions.explanation: Transcription: RNA polymerase binds the gene's promoter (initiation), unzips the DNA, and builds a complementary single-stranded mRNA from the template strand (elongation) until it reaches the terminator and falls off (termination). The mRNA's sequence matches the coding strand, with U instead of T. Translation: ribosomal subunits bind the mRNA at the start codon AUG; tRNAs with complementary anticodons bring amino acids, which are joined by peptide bonds codon by codon; at a stop codon no tRNA binds and the ribosome breaks apart. The amino acid chain (primary structure) then folds into its 3-D shape on its own. The mRNA is destroyed so the protein isn't made nonstop; more can be made by transcribing a new mRNA.
